content:
What Does a Kitchen Remodel Cost in Utah?

The kitchen is the heart of the home — and it's usually the most expensive room to remodel. Whether you're updating a dated kitchen or doing a complete gut renovation, understanding the costs upfront helps you make smart decisions and avoid surprises.

I'm Alan Barben, owner of American Legacy Contracting. I've been remodeling kitchens across Utah County for over 14 years, and I can tell you: no two kitchen projects are the same. But I can give you a solid framework for what to expect in 2026.

Kitchen Remodel Cost Ranges in Utah (2026)

Here's a realistic breakdown of what Utah homeowners are paying this year:

Minor Kitchen Refresh: $10,000 - $25,000

  • Cabinet refacing or painting (not replacing)
  • New countertops
  • Updated hardware and fixtures
  • New backsplash
  • Fresh paint
  • Same layout — no walls moved, no plumbing changes

Mid-Range Kitchen Remodel: $25,000 - $50,000

  • New cabinets (semi-custom or stock)
  • Quartz or granite countertops
  • New flooring throughout the kitchen
  • Updated lighting and electrical
  • New sink and faucet
  • Possible minor layout adjustments
  • New appliances (mid-range brands)

Major Kitchen Renovation: $50,000 - $100,000+

  • Complete layout change (moving walls, plumbing, gas lines)
  • Custom cabinetry
  • Premium countertops (thick-slab quartz, natural stone, or waterfall edges)
  • High-end appliances
  • Custom lighting design
  • New flooring, possibly extending into adjacent rooms
  • Structural changes (removing a wall to open the floor plan)

What Drives the Cost of a Kitchen Remodel?

Cabinets: The Biggest Line Item

Cabinets typically account for 30-40% of your total kitchen remodel budget. Stock cabinets from a home improvement store might run $5,000 to $10,000 for an average kitchen. Semi-custom cabinets push that to $10,000 to $20,000. Fully custom cabinets can easily exceed $25,000.

If your existing cabinets are structurally sound, refacing or painting them is one of the biggest money-savers in a kitchen remodel. A professional paint job on existing cabinets can completely transform the look for a fraction of the replacement cost.

Countertops

Countertop costs vary widely based on material:

  • Laminate: $10-$30 per square foot (installed)
  • Butcher block: $40-$70 per square foot
  • Quartz: $50-$100 per square foot
  • Granite: $50-$100 per square foot
  • Marble: $75-$150+ per square foot

For most Utah homeowners, quartz has become the go-to choice — it's durable, low-maintenance, and available in a huge range of colors and patterns.

Layout Changes

Moving plumbing, gas lines, or electrical is where costs escalate quickly. Relocating a sink or adding a kitchen island with plumbing can add $3,000 to $8,000 or more to your project. Removing a load-bearing wall to open up the floor plan requires a structural beam, which can run $2,000 to $5,000+ depending on the span.

My advice: if you can work within your existing layout, you'll save a significant amount. But if your current layout genuinely doesn't function well, the investment in moving things around is usually worth it in the long run.

Appliances

New appliances can range from $3,000 for a basic package to $15,000+ for premium brands. Keep in mind that switching from electric to gas (or vice versa) requires running new utility lines, which adds to the cost.

Flooring

Kitchen flooring costs depend on the material and square footage. Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) is the most popular choice right now — it's waterproof, durable, and looks great at $3 to $7 per square foot installed. Tile runs $6 to $15+ per square foot, and hardwood is $8 to $15+ per square foot.

Lighting

Don't underestimate the impact of good lighting. Recessed lights, under-cabinet lighting, and pendant lights over an island can completely change how your kitchen feels. Budget $1,500 to $4,000 for a solid lighting upgrade.

Where to Save vs. Where to Splurge

After doing this for 14 years, here's my honest take on where your money makes the biggest impact:

Worth Splurging On

  • Countertops — You touch and see them every day. Quality countertops make the whole kitchen look and feel premium.
  • Cabinet quality — Soft-close hinges, solid construction, and good drawer slides make a daily difference.
  • Layout that works — If your kitchen flow is broken, fixing it is worth every dollar.
  • Good lighting — It's relatively affordable and has an outsized impact on the final result.

Safe to Save On

  • Cabinet hardware — You can find attractive pulls and knobs at very reasonable prices.
  • Backsplash — A simple subway tile looks clean and classic without the cost of intricate mosaic patterns.
  • Appliances — Mid-range appliances from reputable brands perform well. You don't need the $5,000 refrigerator unless you really want it.
  • Sink — A quality stainless steel or composite sink doesn't need to be expensive to look great and last.

Timeline: How Long Does a Kitchen Remodel Take?

A realistic timeline for most kitchen remodels in Utah:

  • Minor refresh: 1 - 3 weeks
  • Mid-range remodel: 4 - 6 weeks
  • Major renovation: 6 - 10 weeks

These timelines assume materials are ordered in advance and permits (if needed) are already in hand. Custom cabinets can have lead times of 4 to 8 weeks before installation even begins, so plan accordingly.

During the remodel, you'll be without a fully functional kitchen. I always recommend setting up a temporary kitchen station — a microwave, coffee maker, and access to a bathroom sink go a long way.

Permits: When Do You Need One?

Not every kitchen remodel requires a permit, but many do. Here's the general rule in Utah:

  • Cosmetic changes only (paint, hardware, countertops, backsplash): No permit needed.
  • Electrical work (adding circuits, moving outlets): Permit required.
  • Plumbing work (moving a sink, adding a gas line): Permit required.
  • Structural changes (removing walls): Permit required.

When you work with a licensed contractor, we handle the permit process for you — pulling the permit, scheduling inspections, and making sure everything passes.

How to Get an Accurate Estimate

  1. Know your goals. Are you refreshing for resale or building your dream kitchen to live in for 20 years? This changes the approach entirely.
  2. Set a realistic budget range. Having a budget in mind helps your contractor design a project that maximizes value without surprises.
  3. Get detailed bids. A good bid breaks down costs by category — demo, cabinets, countertops, plumbing, electrical, flooring, etc. Beware of single-line-item quotes.
  4. Ask about allowances. If a bid lists "countertop allowance: $3,000," find out exactly what that buys. Allowances are estimates, and you might spend more or less.
  5. Plan for the unexpected. Older homes in Utah can have surprises behind walls — outdated wiring, old plumbing, or water damage. A 10-15% contingency fund is smart.
